tagline: Birthplace of steel pan and calypso
overview:
Trinidad and Tobago is a two-island country at the southern end of the Caribbean, so close to South America that Trinidad lies only about 11 kilometers off the coast of Venezuela. Trinidad is the larger, busier island; Tobago, to the northeast, is smaller, greener and quieter. Together they cover about 5,130 km², roughly the size of Delaware.

About 1.4 million people live here, speaking English along with a lively Trinidadian creole. Port of Spain, on Trinidad's northwest coast, is the capital.

The country is a republic with an elected parliament and a president as head of state. Unlike most Caribbean nations it does not depend on tourism: oil, natural gas and petrochemicals make it one of the wealthiest countries in the region. It is best known for Carnival, for inventing the steel pan, and for giving the world calypso and soca music.
landAndNature: Trinidad broke away from South America long ago, so its wildlife is continental rather than island-style: it has ocelots, red howler monkeys, capybaras and around 480 bird species, including scarlet ibis that fly in flocks to roost in the Caroni swamp, turning the mangroves red at sunset. Three mountain ranges cross Trinidad, the tallest reaching about 940 meters. Pitch Lake in the southwest is the world's largest natural deposit of asphalt, a slow-moving pool of tar that visitors can walk on. Tobago is ringed by coral reefs and has a rainforest reserve protected since 1776, thought to be the oldest legally protected forest in the Western Hemisphere. Leatherback turtles nest in large numbers on both islands, and the islands lie mostly south of the main hurricane track.
peopleAndCulture: The population is split roughly evenly between people of Indian and of African descent, with Chinese, European, Syrian-Lebanese and Indigenous roots as well, and holidays include Diwali, Eid, Christmas and Carnival. Carnival, in the days before Lent, is the biggest event: months of preparation lead to costume bands of thousands, calypso and soca competitions, and J'ouvert, a dawn street party in mud and paint. The steel pan, made by hammering oil drums into tuned playing surfaces, was invented here in the 1930s and 1940s and is the national instrument. Food shows the mix: doubles, curried chickpeas in fried bread, is the classic street breakfast, alongside roti, callaloo and pelau. Cricket is the main sport, and Brian Lara scored the highest individual score in Test cricket.
history: Indigenous Arawak and Carib peoples lived on both islands when Columbus arrived in 1498. Spain held Trinidad for nearly 300 years with little development, then invited French planters in the 1780s, which is why many places have French names. Britain took Trinidad in 1797 and had already fought over Tobago, which changed hands among European powers more than twenty times. Enslaved Africans worked sugar and cocoa estates until abolition in 1834; afterward, over 140,000 indentured laborers came from India between 1845 and 1917, reshaping the islands. Oil drilling began early, in 1857. The two islands were joined administratively in 1889. Trinidad and Tobago became independent on August 31, 1962 and a republic in 1976. Its economy has risen and fallen with world energy prices ever since.
funFacts: The steel pan, invented in Trinidad from discarded oil drums, is the only widely played acoustic instrument created in the 20th century.
Pitch Lake holds roughly 10 million tonnes of natural asphalt and has been mined for over a century without running out.
Tobago's Main Ridge Forest Reserve, protected since 1776, is likely the oldest forest reserve in the Western Hemisphere.
The scarlet ibis, one of the country's two national birds, gets its brilliant red color from the crabs it eats.
Trinidad's Carnival costumes can take a year to design and build, and some headpieces stand taller than a person.
